title: Helicopter Operations
description: Key concepts from AIM Chapter 10 covering helicopter IFR operations, offshore operations, and special procedures

cards.back:
Copter Approaches:
• Maximum 90 KIAS (unless charted)
• RNAV final/missed: 70 KIAS max

Conventional Approaches:
• May fly at any Cat A-E speed
• Must slow to ≤90 KIAS at MAP for visibility reduction

Visibility reduction: 1/2 Cat A (min 1/4 SM/1200 RVR)

Two types:

1. 'PROCEED VISUALLY':
• Aligned to landing area (≤30° turn)
• Must see landing area at MAP
• Visual segment evaluated for obstacles

2. 'PROCEED VFR':
• Not aligned to landing area
• Continue VFR from MAP
• Pilot responsible for obstacles

• IFR route structure independent of ground NAVAIDs
• 300+ waypoints, 20 min apart (lat/long)
• 5-letter names derived from position
• Enables IFR to offshore platforms

Approach types:
• OSAP (Offshore Standard Approach)
• HEDA (Helicopter En Route Descent)
• ARA (Airborne Radar Approach)

For IFR certification:

Trim Systems: Cyclic centering (hands-on)
SAS: Stability augmentation (hands-on)
ATT: Attitude retention (hands-off)
Autopilot: Heading, altitude, nav tracking
Flight Director: Visual guidance cues

Different helicopters require different systems for IFR

Recommended minimums:

Small (Bell 206, AS350): 60 x 60 ft
Medium (Bell 412, S-76): 100 x 100 ft
Large (Blackhawk, Chinook): 120 x 120 ft

LZ requirements:
• Level and firm
• Clear of debris, obstructions
• No wires (hard to see from air)

Spectators: 200 feet minimum
Emergency vehicles: 100 feet
Fire equipment: Standing by

Ground personnel:
• Wear eye protection
• Secure helmets (chin straps)
• Remove loose hats
• Wet down dusty LZs
• Clear debris before landing

HIGH LIGHTING:
• Moon ≥50% illuminated AND above horizon
• OR extensive cultural lighting
• OR high natural reflectivity (snow, desert)

LOW LIGHTING:
• Does not meet high lighting criteria
• Increased risk
• Higher minimums recommended

First helicopter:
• Contact ground 10 NM out
• Establish comm on 123.025
• Set up altitudes/orbits for others
• Provide LZ briefing

Subsequent helicopters:
• Contact 123.025 at 10 NM
• Maintain 500 ft separation
• Monitor 123.025 at all times

123.025 MHz

Used for:
• EMS coordination at scenes
• Multiple helicopter operations
• Hospital heliport coordination
• Offshore operations

Announce position and intentions before LZ movement

Unique challenges:
• Weather (fog, wind, sea state)
• Platform obstacles (cranes, flares)
• Limited landing areas
• Coordination with oil/gas operations

Key practices:
• Passenger briefings
• Crane coordination
• Platform lighting requirements
• Emergency procedures

FATO: Final Approach and Takeoff Area
TLOF: Touchdown and Liftoff Area
HILS: Heliport Instrument Lighting System
HALS: Heliport Approach Lighting System
VGSI: Visual Glideslope Indicator

At least one must be visible for 'Proceed Visually'

Visual segment departure:
1. Establish hover at HCH (Heliport Crossing Height)
2. Depart on published heading
3. Climb ≥400 ft/NM (or charted)
4. Remain clear of clouds
5. Cross IDF at/above published altitude

VFR segment: Pilot navigation to IDF

Cranes near heliports:
• Must be lowered during operations
• Boom and load clear of approach path
• Communication required
• Radio contact established

Catastrophic consequences possible if procedures not followed

On conventional (non-Copter) approaches:

Helicopters may reduce Cat A visibility by half:
• Minimum: 1/4 SM or 1200 RVR
• MDA/DA: NO reduction allowed
• Must slow to ≤90 KIAS at MAP

NA if charted 'Visibility Reduction by Helicopters NA'

Before arrival:
• Contact comm center/flight following
• Get permission and current conditions
• Know primary/secondary routes
• Know orbit area if occupied

Multiple helicopters:
• First notify of departure time
• Coordinate on 123.025
• Follow local procedures
